title: System Performance: Load, CPU, Memory, and I/O
intro: 'The server is slow' can mean CPU, memory, disk I/O, or something else entirely. These tools tell you which one within the first minute — before you waste time guessing.

steps.prompt: Check the load average and how long the system has been up.
steps.explanation: Load averages over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It jumped sharply recently (2.05 → 7.82).
steps.why: Load only means something relative to CPU count — check next. A load of 7.8 is fine on 16 cores and severe on 2.

steps.prompt: Check how many CPU cores this machine has.
steps.explanation: Only 2 cores against a load of 7.8 — processes are queuing badly.
steps.why: Comparing load average to nproc is the fastest sanity check there is. Load consistently above core count means work is waiting.

steps.prompt: Get a per-second snapshot of CPU, memory, swap, and I/O wait — 5 samples, 1 second apart.
steps.fake_output:
procs -----memory---- ---swap-- -----io---- ---cpu---
 r  b   free  cache  si  so   bi    bo  us sy id wa
 1  6  81200 204000   0   0  9800  4200  5  3 12 80
steps.explanation: The key column is 'wa' = 80: CPUs spend 80% of their time WAITING on disk I/O, not computing. 'b' = 6 processes blocked on I/O.
steps.why: High load with high 'us' (user CPU) means compute-bound; high load with high 'wa' means disk-bound. They need completely different fixes — adding CPU won't help an I/O problem at all.

steps.prompt: It's disk-bound. See which disk is saturated.
steps.explanation: sda is at 99.8% utilization with 112ms average wait per request — completely saturated by writes.
steps.why: %util near 100% plus a high await is the signature of a saturated disk. Now the question becomes WHO is writing so much, which tools like 'iotop' or checking recently-growing logs answer.

steps.prompt: Check the kernel log for hardware errors or OOM events, with human-readable timestamps.
steps.fake_output:
[Sat Sep 27 10:38:12 2026] EXT4-fs warning (device sda1): ext4_dx_add_entry: Directory index full!
[Sat Sep 27 10:39:44 2026] app invoked oom-killer
steps.explanation: The kernel log shows things applications never see: filesystem warnings, hardware errors, and OOM kills.
steps.why: dmesg is where the OOM killer leaves its evidence — if a process vanished with no error in its own logs, dmesg is the first place to look. -T converts kernel uptime-seconds into real clock times.
